text: Windows doesn't speak syslog natively — its event logs live in a proprietary binary format read through Event Viewer, not plaintext lines a syslog listener can parse. Windows Event Forwarding, or WEF, is Microsoft's built-in answer: a subscription-based mechanism that moves events between Windows machines without installing any third-party agent, and it ships with Windows itself at no extra cost.

WEF runs on top of WinRM, Windows Remote Management, over TCP port 5985 for HTTP or 5986 for HTTPS. A central Windows Event Collector server defines a subscription specifying which events, like failed logons on Event ID 4625, to collect and from which source computers. Forwarded events land in a dedicated log on the collector called ForwardedEvents, which a SIEM or an agent sitting on that collector can then read and ship onward into the platform.

There are two subscription models. Source-initiated, or push, uses a Group Policy Object to tell hundreds or thousands of machines at once to start forwarding — the common choice at scale because it needs no per-machine setup. Collector-initiated, or pull, flips that: the collector itself maintains the source list and reaches out to each machine, which suits a smaller, more tightly controlled set of servers.

WEF isn't the only path. A dedicated forwarding agent — Splunk's Universal Forwarder, Winlogbeat, QRadar's WinCollect, Azure Monitor Agent — is lightweight software installed on each endpoint instead. WEF needs no extra software and uses infrastructure Windows already has, but it's Windows-only and adds GPO configuration to get right. An agent can forward to almost any SIEM and works cross-platform, at the cost of one more install to deploy and maintain on every host.

Many SOCs run both: WEF to consolidate branch-office servers into a regional collector, then one forwarding agent on that collector to reach the SIEM. Neither choice is universally correct — it depends on what's already deployed and what the destination SIEM understands.
